topic: The Aral Sea: how a sea was lost, and how part of it came back
method: Web searches (13 queries) on the sea's size, the river diversions, the split, the 2014 drying, the Aralkum, salinity, dust, the fisheries, Moynaq, the Kok-Aral dike, water levels and the North Aral's recovery. The source pages themselves could not be opened from the research environment (the hosts are not reachable there), so every 'quote' below is the search engine's summary of the page, marked [summary]; figures were used only where independent results agreed, or are attributed in the narration to the one source that gives them. Areas were also measured independently from Natural Earth's public-domain outlines (C25), which agree with NASA's figure.

claims.claim: Before its decline the Aral Sea covered about 68,000 square kilometres and was among the four largest lakes in the world.

sources.title: Aral Sea (Wikipedia, mirror)
sources.quote: [summary] 1960 surface area of 68,000 km2 (26,300 sq mi), before it split into separate lakes

sources.title: NASA finds that Earth's fourth-largest lake is almost completely dry (The Week)
sources.quote: [summary] formerly the fourth largest lake in the world

sources.title: Once-Massive Aral Sea Is Drying Up (Live Science)
sources.quote: [summary] once the fourth-largest lake on Earth

claims.claim: The sea began shrinking after the Soviet Union diverted the Syr Darya and Amu Darya rivers for irrigation, chiefly for cotton, from the 1950s and 1960s.

sources.title: The Aral Sea Loses Its Eastern Lobe (NASA Earth Observatory)
sources.quote: [summary] shrinkage began after the Soviet Union started diverting water from the Syr Darya and the Amu Darya in the 1950s and 1960s

sources.title: The Disappearing Aral Sea (Resources for the Future)
sources.quote: [summary] the rivers that feed it were diverted by the Soviet Union for irrigation

sources.title: Desiccation of the Aral Sea (Seventeen Moments in Soviet History, MSU)
sources.quote: [summary] the Karakum Canal was a centerpiece of Soviet plans to expand cotton production in the central Asian republics

claims.claim: The amount of water taken from the rivers doubled between 1960 and 1980, and cotton production nearly doubled in the same period.

sources.title: The Disappearing Aral Sea (Resources for the Future)
sources.quote: [summary] the amount of water taken from the rivers doubled between 1960 and 1980; cotton production nearly doubled in the same period

claims.claim: By some estimates only 20 to 25 percent of the water diverted from the rivers was actually used by the crops.

sources.title: The Disappearing Aral Sea (Resources for the Future)
sources.quote: [summary] some estimates say only 20 to 25% of the water diverted from the rivers is actually used by the crops

claims.claim: As the level fell, the sea split into a small northern sea and a large southern sea in the late 1980s (sources give 1987 to 1989).

sources.title: North Aral Sea (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: [summary] the North Aral Sea split from the South Aral Sea in 1987-1988

sources.title: Aral Sea (Aquapedia, Water Diplomacy)
sources.quote: [summary] by 1989, the northern part of the Aral Sea had essentially split from the southern part

sources.title: JAXA Earth View
sources.quote: [summary] the Aral Sea separated into north and south areas in the second half of the 1980s

claims.claim: In August 2014 NASA imagery showed the eastern basin of the South Aral completely dry for the first time in modern history; the geographer Philip Micklin said it was likely the first time in about 600 years.

sources.title: The Aral Sea Loses Its Eastern Lobe (NASA Earth Observatory)
sources.quote: [summary] for the first time in modern history, the eastern basin of the South Aral Sea has completely dried ... likely the first time it has completely dried in 600 years (Philip Micklin, Western Michigan University)

sources.title: Aral Sea's eastern basin has dried out, NASA photos show (WGBH)
sources.quote: [summary] For the first time in modern history, the eastern basin of the South Aral Sea has completely dried.

sources.title: Disappearing Lakes: Most Of Aral Sea Is Gone (Lake Scientist)
sources.quote: [summary] the eastern basin is gone

claims.claim: Since the 1960s the sea has shrunk to roughly 10 percent of its original area.

sources.title: Dunes and Desert Replace the Aral Sea (NASA Earth Observatory)
sources.quote: [summary] since the 1960s, it has decreased to approximately 10 percent of its original area

sources.title: Report reveals world's fourth largest lake now a deadly desert (ScienceAlert)
sources.quote: [summary] the sea has lost most of its area; the former seabed is now desert

claims.claim: The exposed seabed is now a desert, the Aralkum, described as the youngest desert in the world.

sources.title: Aralkum Desert (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: [summary] the Aralkum, which is the youngest desert in the world

sources.title: The youngest desert on Earth - Aralkum is growing (Central Asia Climate Portal)
sources.quote: [summary] the youngest desert on Earth is growing in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan

sources.title: Dunes and Desert Replace the Aral Sea (NASA Earth Observatory)
sources.quote: [summary] dunes and desert replace the Aral Sea

contradictions: Its size is given as 62,000 km2 by one source and 54,000 km2 by IFAS; the film does not state a size.

claims.claim: Salinity rose as the water left: about 10 grams per litre in 1947 and about 90 g/l in 2002 (Marburg study); a 2022 report gives about 170 g/l for the western South Aral and 10-14 g/l for the North Aral. Ocean water is about 35 g/l.

sources.title: Dust deposition study, University of Marburg
sources.quote: [summary] about 10.2 g/l in 1947 and 90 g/l in 2002

sources.title: Analytical report, Aral Sea Study (BES-Net)
sources.quote: [summary] 170 g/l for the Western Aral Sea and 10-14 g/l for the Northern Aral Sea

claims.claim: Dust storms lift salt, fertiliser and pesticide residues from the Aralkum; one study found dust in the region nearly doubled between 1984 and 2015.

sources.title: Dust deposition study, University of Marburg
sources.quote: [summary] storms carry salts, heavy metals and agrochemicals from the Aralkum

sources.title: Report reveals world's fourth largest lake now a deadly desert (ScienceAlert)
sources.quote: [summary] a 2015 study found dust in the region nearly doubled between 1984 and 2015

claims.claim: The dust has been linked to respiratory and other illness in the region, but much of the evidence comes from news reports rather than peer-reviewed epidemiology.

sources.title: Pollution, health issues and fishing on the Aral Sea (Facts and Details)
sources.quote: [summary] the dust is linked to respiratory and eye disorders, birth defects, anaemia and cancers

sources.title: Aral Sea desiccation (EBSCO Research Starters)
sources.quote: [summary] shrinkage linked to dust storms and sharply rising mortality and morbidity rates

contradictions: The health claims come mostly from news and popular sites rather than peer-reviewed epidemiology, and specific case counts are not well sourced.

claims.claim: In 1957 the Aral's fisheries landed about 48,000 tonnes of fish.

sources.title: Moynak - Memories of the Aral Sea (Caspian Post)
sources.quote: [summary] in 1957, 48,000 tons of fish were landed

contradictions: Another account gives about 100 million pounds (45,000 tonnes) a year in the late 1950s, which is consistent.

claims.claim: Estimates of employment in the Aral fisheries at their height range from about 30,000 to 60,000 people; 40,000 is often cited.

sources.title: Moynak - Memories of the Aral Sea (Caspian Post)
sources.quote: [summary] the Aral fishing industry in its heyday had employed some 40,000

sources.title: The Ship Graveyard (ipernity)
sources.quote: [summary] the Moynaq harbour and fishing industry employed approximately 30,000 people

contradictions: One source says 60,000; another 30,000; a Soviet-era article says 10,000 fishermen worked out of Moynaq alone. No scholarly figure was found.

claims.claim: Late in its life the Moynaq cannery processed fish brought from the Baltic Sea and the Pacific Ocean, until it closed around 1990.

sources.title: Moynak - Memories of the Aral Sea (Caspian Post)
sources.quote: [summary] the cannery processed fish delivered in refrigerated trucks from the Baltic Sea and the Pacific Ocean until it finally closed that year in 1990

claims.claim: Moynaq in Uzbekistan was a port on the Aral Sea; abandoned fishing ships now lie on the former port site, the 'ship graveyard'.

sources.title: Open-air Museum (Ship Graveyard), Karakalpakstan tourism
sources.quote: [summary] formed on the site of former Muynak Port

sources.title: Ship Graveyard - Muynak - former fishing port on the Aral Sea
sources.quote: [summary] Muynak, a former fishing port on the Aral Sea

sources.title: The Muynak Ship Graveyard (Abandoned in 360)
sources.quote: [summary] the ship graveyard of the former port

claims.claim: Moynaq is now roughly 100 kilometres or more from the shoreline; travel sources give figures from about 100 to 130 km depending on the point measured.

sources.title: Getting to Aral Sea (Eurasia Travel)
sources.quote: [summary] the current shoreline is an additional 100 km of off-road travel from Muynak

sources.title: Muynak (Uzbek Travel)
sources.quote: [summary] Muynak is now about 100 kilometers away from the shoreline

contradictions: Another route description gives about 130 km from Muynak to a camp on the shore.

claims.claim: In August 2005 Kazakhstan completed the Kok-Aral dike, about 13 km (8 miles) long, with World Bank help, separating the North Aral from the South.

sources.title: Saving a Corner of the Aral Sea (World Bank)
sources.quote: [summary] the dam was finished in August 2005 with World Bank help

sources.title: Dike Kokaral (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: [summary] the Kokaral Dam, a roughly 12 km barrier, splitting off the North Aral Sea

sources.title: Kazakhstan fights to save its corner of a divided Aral Sea (The Ecologist)
sources.quote: [summary] an eight-mile dam on the northern sea's southern shore

claims.claim: Water levels: about 53.4 m above sea level in 1960; the North (Small) Aral about 42 m by 2008-2009; the South (Large) Aral about 26.5 m in September 2009 (Micklin's data).

sources.title: P. Micklin, presentation, Aral 2009 conference
sources.quote: [summary] 1960 level 53.4 meters, 1090 km3 of volume; Large Sea = 26.5 meters; Small Sea = 42 meters

sources.title: JAXA Earth View
sources.quote: [summary] 53.41m in 1960

sources.title: North Aral Sea (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: [summary] by 2008, the water level had risen ... to 42 m

contradictions: Another summary gives 29 m for the South Aral in 2007; officials quoted elsewhere give the North's pre-dike level as under 30 m or 38 m.

claims.claim: According to Kazakhstan's fisheries research institute, the North Aral catch grew from 695 tonnes in 2005 to 5,595 tonnes in 2014.

sources.title: Kazakhstan: Measuring the Northern Aral's comeback (Eurasianet)
sources.quote: [summary] data from the Kazakh Research Institute of Fisheries shows the Small Aral catch grew from 695 metric tons in 2005 to 5,595 tons in 2014

claims.claim: A 2026 report says the North Aral fish catch fell in 2025 from about 7,800 to 3,900 tonnes as the water line receded.

sources.title: How Kazakhstan resurrected the North Aral Sea (Global Voices)
sources.quote: [summary] fish catch fell in 2025, from 7.8 to 3.9 thousand tons, and the receding water line underscore the precariousness of this victory

claims.claim: A second phase of the project plans to rebuild the dike and raise the North Aral to 44 metres.

sources.title: Kazakhstan and World Bank launch second phase to revive Northern Aral Sea (Times of Central Asia)
sources.quote: [summary] key objectives of this phase include reconstructing the Kokaral Dam and raising the sea level to 44 meters

claims.claim: Whether Soviet planners foresaw or accepted the loss of the sea when the irrigation schemes began is disputed.

sources.title: Desiccation of the Aral Sea (Seventeen Moments in Soviet History, MSU)
sources.quote: [summary] the Soviet government's long-term plan for the Aral Sea when they started the irrigation work in the 1960s remains disputed

contradictions: A Soviet engineer is quoted (1968) saying the evaporation of the Aral Sea was inevitable; the original source of the quote was not found.

claims.claim: Measured from Natural Earth's public-domain lake outlines, the Aral Sea's historic extent is about 67,500 km2 and today's North and South Aral together about 6,800 km2 (roughly 10 percent), consistent with C01 and C08.

sources.title: Natural Earth 1:10m lakes and historic lakes
sources.quote: [summary] public-domain vector outlines; areas computed by the studio from the outlines

claims.claim: Terrain is drawn from open elevation tiles (Mapzen / AWS Terrain Tiles); heights are exaggerated and the factor is shown on screen.

sources.title: Terrain Tiles on AWS Open Data
sources.quote: [summary] global elevation tiles combining SRTM, GMTED, ETOPO1 and other sources

claims.claim: The Aral Sea has no outlet to the ocean: it is fed by the Amu Darya and Syr Darya and loses water by evaporation.

sources.title: Aral Sea (Wikipedia, mirror)
sources.quote: [summary] an endorheic lake fed by the Amu Darya and Syr Darya

sources.title: Aral Sea (Aquapedia, Water Diplomacy)
sources.quote: [summary] a terminal lake whose level depends on river inflow and evaporation

claims.claim: The South Aral, outside the dike, has kept shrinking; it split again into east and west around 2000.

sources.title: North Aral Sea (Wikipedia)
sources.quote: [summary] the south ... remains almost completely desiccated due to ongoing agricultural and industrial drainage

sources.title: JAXA Earth View
sources.quote: [summary] it separated into east and west areas around the year 2000 and is continuing to shrink

claims.claim: The film's reading: the sea was lost to decisions about where river water goes, not to a natural drought; the North Aral shows part of that can be reversed and how fragile the reversal is.

sources.title: The Aral Sea Loses Its Eastern Lobe (NASA Earth Observatory)
sources.quote: [summary] shrinkage began after diversion of the rivers

sources.title: How Kazakhstan resurrected the North Aral Sea (Global Voices)
sources.quote: [summary] the precariousness of this victory
